items.title: Otters raise hope for Kuala Lumpur’s river
items.summary: Smooth-coated otters are increasingly being spotted along Kuala Lumpur’s Klang River, raising hopes that years of clean-up efforts are improving water quality and restoring urban wildlife habitats. However, their growing presence is not without conflict. Habitat loss caused by development has driven some otters into residential areas, where they have raided fish ponds, prompting calls for residents to adapt rather than harm these protected animals. Conservationists and city officials hope the otters can encourage further efforts to clean up the Klang, reduce waste entering the river and restore more natural riverbanks. Read the full storyThis article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Otters raise hope for Kuala Lumpur’s river

items.title: What’s the most sustainable way to eat fish? Forget it. There isn’t one | George Monbiot
items.summary:
Don’t take the bait offered up by ‘conservation’ charities. Fishing is about as good for our ecosystems as tobacco is for our health

Drumroll please. I am about to unveil the species of fish that’s best to eat if you want to protect the living seas. Ta-dah! It’s … I hope that clears things up. Unfortunately, over the past few years, a noisy industry has developed to tell you otherwise. You’re doing the planet a favour if you eat mackerel, sorry, cod, I mean haddock, no coley, make that pollack – oh, whoops! These choices might make you feel better about yourself. But they do nothing but harm to marine wildlife. The fish you should choose is none of the above.

Cause, could I introduce you to effect? In April, the Marine Conservation Society, through its Good Fish Guide, suggested you stop eating cod and eat hake instead. Six months later, it lamented that hake is now overexploited thanks to “increased fishing pressure”, and…
items.t: What’s the most sustainable way to eat fish? Forget it. There isn’t one | George Monbiot

items.title: Country diary: Stalked by a herd of ghostly white deer | Mary Montague
items.summary:
Parkanaur Forest Park, County Tyrone: The autumn rut is over, and I meet the eye of a patriarch male as it surveys his extended family

Emerging from a dip in the hillside, the deer’s antlers crown a white head that nods with the stilted grace of his stride. Through the oak trees, he meets my gaze. A raven kroks. I blink. Then the fallow buck’s ghostly form strolls on over the rise.

White deer are a potent symbol across cultures. Celtic mythology interpreted them as messengers from the “Otherworld”. Medieval legend tells of how a white hart (buck or stag) drew Camelot’s King Arthur into the dark…
items.t: Country diary: Stalked by a herd of ghostly white deer | Mary Montague

items.title: Deadly accidents loom over labor dispute at Indonesia’s largest nickel hub
items.summary: Since it was established in 2015, PT Indonesia Morowali Industrial Park, the world’s largest conglomeration of nickel smelters, has sat at the heart of Indonesia’s ambition to choke off exports of raw resources and force exporters to instead process the ore at home. Majority-owned by China’s Tsingshan Holding Group and home to more than 50 companies and more than 100,000 workers, the industrial park, known as IMIP, processes nickel into stainless steel and the basic materials that go into making batteries for electric vehicles and storage for solar and other intermittent sources of renewable energy. It may also be among Indonesia’s most dangerous industrial places to work. How dangerous, though, is a matter of debate. Unions, representing about 10,000 workers, including those in IMIP smelters, have said they won’t sign on to a collective bargaining agreement, or CBA, in part because employers won’t allow them to participate on health and safety committees that file formal incident reports. The issue has been a live one since December 2023, when a deadly blast at a nickel smelter furnace owned by Indonesia Tsingshan Stainless Steel, a Tsingshan subsidiary, ultimately claimed the lives of 21 workers. On Nov. 7 this year, unions, including the Federation of Independent Industrial Workers’ Unions (FSPIM), the Indonesian Morowali Industrial Labor Union (SBIMI), and the Mining and Energy Industry Labor Unions (SBIPE), called off a five day sit-in at government labor department offices in Morowali district, Central Sulawesi province. The sit-in had been launched in a bid, union…
items.t: Deadly accidents loom over labor dispute at Indonesia’s largest nickel hub

items.title: Study reveals rising ‘double threat’ of wildfire smoke and heatwaves in Indonesia
items.summary: JAKARTA — While the worst of Indonesia’s wildfire and haze season for 2026 may be over with fewer hotspots detected in recent weeks, this wasn’t the only hazard faced by residents in the months-long crisis. Take, for example, Palangka Raya in Central Kalimantan province, one of the areas worst affected by this year’s wildfires in the country. From August to October 2026, fine-particle pollution in the provincial capital averaged nearly 10 times the 2021 to 2025 level, according to data from Indonesia’s meteorological agency, BMKG. Meanwhile, as haze choked the city in August, its residents also experienced a heatwave, according to data from BMKG. Exposure to wildfire air pollution and heatwaves on the same days has become more common globally, according to a new study published in the journal Science Advances. Researchers from Monash University, in Melbourne, Australia, analyzed 20 years of data, from 2000 to 2019, and found that, on average, 916 million people, or 56% of the global population, experienced one co-exposure day annually. The total number of people increased by 287 million from one decade to the next, according to the study. The top five countries worst affected were the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Indonesia, Mexico, Brazil and Russia. The study blamed the double exposure on climate change, saying it “has increased the frequency and intensity of concurrent heatwaves and landscape fire events, resulting in more profound impacts.” A student goes to school wearing a mask in the haze that blankets the city of Palangka Raya,…This article was…
items.t: Study reveals rising ‘double threat’ of wildfire smoke and heatwaves in Indonesia

items.title: Species down to the last 50 animals can recover, but rarely without help
items.summary: In 1974, the Mauritius kestrel was down to four birds in the wild. In 1979, Norman Myers, a prominent environmentalist, argued that the money might be better spent protecting birds with better prospects. Nevertheless, conservationists pursued captive breeding, predator control, and releases of the Mauritius kestrel (Falco punctatus). Its numbers eventually recovered into the hundreds, though the population has since declined again. The Mauritius kestrel is one of 141 species examined in a study published in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B. The researchers, led by Donal Smith of Monash University in Australia, looked at birds and mammals whose wild populations had fallen below 50 individuals at some point since 1950, and for which enough time had passed to assess the outcome. Of the 51 species that received direct conservation help, 31 (61%) recovered to at least 100 individuals. Six went extinct. Among the 90 species without direct intervention, just two (2%) reached a population of 100, while 33 (37%) went extinct. Recoveries were most common when conservationists addressed the causes of decline, such as introduced predators or habitat loss, while also increasing animal numbers through captive breeding or translocation. Legal protection and other indirect measures, on their own, showed no clear association with recovery. The researchers say they can’t establish how much of the recovery was caused by conservation intervention. Some species may have received help because their problems were easier to solve. Reaching 100 animals is hardly a guarantee of survival,…
items.t: Species down to the last 50 animals can recover, but rarely without help

items.title: ‘We don’t want it’: First Nations reject plan to release mining waste into water source
items.summary: Suncor, Canada’s second-largest oil company, wants to release treated wastewater from mining oil in Alberta’s tar sands into a drinking water source for the community of Fort Chipewyan. Investigative reporter Leana Hosea visited the community to learn more. She joins the Mongabay Newscast this week to detail what she found. “This story is not about pro-oil and anti-oil. It’s about waste, not wanting toxic waste, which they don’t know how well it’s going to be treated,” Hosea says. “It’s never happened before. Being released into the Athabasca River, which flows into Lake Athabasca, which is where [the community] all drink from. And because treatment is difficult, it’s uncertain whether they’re going to be able to clean the water to those standards.” While Suncor never responded to Hosea’s request for an interview, Chief Allan Adam of the Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation was told the treated wastewater, or tailings, was “too corrosive” to be used on the oil refinery machinery. While the provincial government of Alberta backs the strategy to release the tailings without an environmental impact assessment, the federal government of Canada will have the final say. In August 2026, Chief Adam wrote to the federal government, urging it to intervene. “When I ran for chief, I was given a mandate of what I needed to get accomplished. I was not given the mandate to agree to a treat and release of a tailings pond, which is deadly toxic. No, we don’t want it,” he told Hosea. Independently, the federal government…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: ‘We don’t want it’: First Nations reject plan to release mining waste into water source

items.title: How a feminist lens is shaping my climate reporting (commentary)
items.summary: In university, I took a unit called Environmental Journalism, taught by one of my favorite lecturers. I paid enough attention to pass, but certainly not enough to imagine it becoming a beat I would want to report on. I could not picture myself willingly sifting through scientific research papers, trying to understand ribosomes or learning about yet another strange species discovered somewhere in the sea. So, when I passed the unit, I thought that was it. Science be damned. I went on to pursue what I was passionate about: women. Their health, economies, livelihoods, rights and the ways power shaped their lives. In June 2024, after torrential floods had damaged parts of Nairobi, I attended a focus group discussion in Kibera as part of conversations about women’s experiences of climate change. The women spoke about the floods, but they also described the extreme heat they endured in iron-sheet homes where temperatures could become unbearable. Some talked about the strain of heat, long hours of manual labor and the frustrations that followed, and how these pressures affected their moods and relationships. Women with disabilities described heightened risks of sexual violence during floods, including instances in which violence was disguised as “help” while crossing pools of water or accessing transport in flooded areas. Those accounts stayed with me because women described how environmental conditions entered the most intimate parts of their lives: their homes, bodies, relationships, safety and ability to earn a living. Their accounts were not evidence that heat causes…
items.t: How a feminist lens is shaping my climate reporting (commentary)

items.title: Why white-tailed sea eagles are a danger to Britain’s seabirds | Letters
items.summary:
The reintroduction of the birds in England and Wales spells disaster for fragile marine ecosystems, warns Tim Birkhead

Your article on white-tailed sea eagle reintroduction (Reintroduction of white-tailed eagles puts seabird colonies at risk of wipeout, say experts, 8 November) highlighted the risk that white-tailed sea eagles are likely to pose to Britain’s seabirds. To argue, as Prof Ian Convery and Rebecca Wrigley did in their responses (Letters, 15 November), that the re-establishment of white-tailed sea eagles will somehow restore a lost paradise is fallacious. Where is the evidence that sea eagles will restore that balance? There is no evidence.

Also, suggesting that because in the distant past sea eagles and seabirds coexisted, their reintroduction will pose no problems is naive. By failing to acknowledge that past marine ecosystems were much more robust, and seabird prey more abundant, than they are today, these two authors miss the point that it is precisely because our seabirds are currently short of food that they are so vulnerable to disturbance and predation from white-tailed sea eagles.

Continue reading...
items.t: Why white-tailed sea eagles are a danger to Britain’s seabirds | Letters

items.title: Clouded tiger cats are notoriously hard to catch. This young researcher caught seven
items.summary: Tadeu de Oliveira, founder and leader of the Tiger Cats Conservation Initiative, a group of scientists committed to studying the smallest wildcats of South and Central America, wanted to be crystal clear: “It is rare to catch a tiger cat. Period. Period!” he emphasized in a phone interview from Brazil with Mongabay. “You may ask ‘what species of tiger cat?’ because there are several. And I would say: all of them! We don’t have much information.” That’s about to change for at least one tiger cat, Leopardus pardinoides oncilla, a resident of the montane cloud forests of Central America. A young scientist, Amaia Autor, a Ph.D. student in conservation biology at the University of Montana in the U.S., has been in relentless pursuit, determined to trap the rare, elusive L. p. oncilla — also known as the clouded tiger cat or clouded oncilla — in the rugged Talamanca Mountains of Costa Rica since mid-2022, according to her Ph.D. adviser, conservation biologist Mark Hebblewhite. In what is being called a research first, Autor has managed to not just capture, evaluate, and collar one oncilla specimen, but seven different specimens since her first trapping in March 2023. She’s now analyzing her research data back in Montana for her doctorate. “Indeed, Amaia is the first person to capture free-ranging individuals of this species for research purposes and to conduct telemetry studies [GPS tracking],” Natalie Montera, a wildlife veterinarian with Cuatro Gatos Conservación (CGC), a Costa Rican initiative, confirmed for Mongabay in an email.…This article was originally published on…
items.t: Clouded tiger cats are notoriously hard to catch. This young researcher caught seven

items.title: Army: Entire U.S. stockpile of lead azide is at Iowa plant and set to be detonated Wednesday morning
items.summary: MIDDLETOWN, Iowa (AP) — The U.S. Army says it plans to detonate its entire stockpile of lead azide in Iowa on Wednesday morning, warning that the dangerously degrading bomb-making chemicals could spread toxic lead within the area. Officials sought to assure residents Tuesday that they’ve taken steps to put barriers around the blast zone and limit the plume from the detonation. “We don’t believe that the public should be in a panic,” said Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle. The controlled detonation of five tons of degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown has set off concerns about potential health and environmental effects and frustration over a lack of information. By Laura Bargfeld and Susan Montoya Bryan, Associated Press Banner image: This photo provided by the U.S. Army shows the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, on May 14, 2024. Image courtesy of Shawn Eldridge/U.S. Army via Associated Press. This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Army: Entire U.S. stockpile of lead azide is at Iowa plant and set to be detonated Wednesday morning

items.title: Ecuador’s bioeconomy plan vows sustainability, but faces a test of government priorities
items.summary: The government of Ecuador has approved a new 10-year plan to promote economic activities that make use of the country’s biological resources, while also taking steps to conserve the ecosystems that they rely on. It aims to innovate agribusiness, ecotourism, and other industries in rural areas, without threatening the environment or Indigenous communities. The National Bioeconomy Strategy, approved on Oct. 29 and to be implemented through 2036, is billed as a new development model that will “align the country’s biological wealth with production, innovation, science and technology.” “Ecuador faces a historic opportunity to redefine the direction of its development, pursuing a model that reconciles natural wealth, territorial equity and innovation with the well-being of its people,” the strategy says. Other parts of the world already have robust bioeconomy strategies. The European Union generates billions of dollars from sustainable farming practices, biomass management, and biotechnology research. In Latin America, the bioeconomy programs in Colombia and Costa Rica have developed ecotourism with Indigenous communities and improved waste management practices in the private sector, among other initiatives. A hammerhead shark nursery in Santa Cruz, Galapagos Islands, Ecuador. Image via Galapagos National Park Photo via AP, File By comparison, Ecuador’s bioeconomy projects are more “scattered” and “isolated,” the strategy acknowledges. The next 10 years will be largely devoted to identifying financing sources for future projects and improving coordination between different parts…
items.t: Ecuador’s bioeconomy plan vows sustainability, but faces a test of government priorities

items.title: As new season starts, Antarctic krill-fishing vessels face urgent conservation decision (commentary)
items.summary: Despite promising developments, the 27 member states of the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR) have again failed to reach an agreement that protects the Southern Ocean. Mired by consensus decision-making and shrouded from public view by confidentiality rules, Antarctica’s governance systems are no longer fulfilling their mandate. This leaves room for private industry to step up and put their money where their mouth is. The Antarctic krill fishery is permitted to extract up to 620,000 metric tons of krill each season. Conservation Measure 51-07 previously split up that quota across smaller fishing subareas. The purpose was to reduce the risk that fishing would be concentrated too heavily in regions where predators depend on krill, as that can cause localized depletion of prey and therefore starvation. Since 2024, due to the expiration of Conservation Measure 51-07 with no replacement, the 620,000-metric-ton krill-fishing catch limits in the northern Antarctic Peninsula have had no spatial distribution. The industry has been free to fish as much as it wants, wherever it wants, even in crucial wildlife breeding and foraging areas. A new report by one of this commentary’s co-author’s organizations — the Antarctic Wildlife Alliance — and Global Fishing Watch demonstrates the massive increase of fishing intensity in vulnerable, biodiversity-rich parts of the Antarctic Peninsula in the last two seasons. Antarctic krill (Euphausia superba) grow to about 5 centimeters long and have historically been present in huge numbers across the…
items.t: As new season starts, Antarctic krill-fishing vessels face urgent conservation decision (commentary)

items.title: This Artist Was Getting Anxious From The News, So He Started Illustrating The Good Stories Instead (30 Pics)
items.summary:
Back in 2018, Italian illustrator Mauro Gatti noticed that the steady stream of grim headlines was making him anxious. Instead of tuning out, the Emmy-winning creative director (the award came for his work on the children’s series StoryBots) went looking for the stories that rarely make the front page. That search became The Happy Broadcast, a project he created to counter the culture of hate and fear with fact-checked, “anxiety-free” news from around the world. 

Every post pairs a real story with one of Gatti’s signature drawings: simple, round-faced characters and cheerful creatures set against bold, bright backgrounds. The formula clearly works. The Instagram page now has over 807,000 followers and more than 1,500 posts. The idea has also grown into a TikTok account, a 2020 book and WHOLE, a mental wellness app the artist runs with his business partner Keith Bonnici. 

Animal rights were among the topics Gatti wanted to see covered from the start, and his book even features a cuddle club that pairs senior dogs with elderly people. For this collection, we’ve picked 30 animal-related illustrations from The Happy Broadcast. They range from new laws protecting cats and dogs to daring rescues, progress in veterinary care and lost pets making their way home. Scroll down to see what’s been going right for animals lately, and follow The Happy Broadcast on Instagram if you’d like more of this kind of news between the usual headlines. 

More info: Instagram | Facebook

items.t: 30 Times “The Happy Broadcast” Shared Good News About Animals That Might Restore Your Hope In People

items.title: In the Bolivian Andes, Indigenous women plant native trees to restore water sources
items.summary: The bare ridges of the Tunari mountain range rise high in Bolivia’s central Cochabamba department. Only the occasional stand of squat, shrubby trees and rust-red potato crops dot the slopes. It wasn’t always this way. The high-elevation landscape was once filled with native Kewiña (Polylepis sp.) trees, a slow-growing tree belonging to the rose family that thrives well above the typical tree line, at up to around 4,450 meters (14,600 feet) above sea level. Today’s lack of vegetation reflects decades of clearing for firewood, construction and small-scale potato agriculture, as well as drier and warmer weather in the area linked to forest loss and climate change. Only 10% of the region’s original Kewiña tree coverage remains, biologists estimate. The trees were also decimated by urban expansion, intensifying wildfires and habitat fragmentation. In 2023, the IUCN listed one Polylepis species endemic to central Bolivia as endangered. Tunari National Park, covering about 309,000 hectares (763,500 acres), is home to a large, albeit much reduced, Kewiña population, which provide vital habitat for the near threatened Cochabamba mountain finch (Poospiza garleppi) as well as critical ecosystem services for the Cochabamba metropolitan area and beyond, to the nearby Amazon basin. Today, however, the region faces both chronic drought and increasing erosion on the mountain range’s slopes. A river bordered by Polylepis trees in Chiaraje, Bolivia, in Tunari National Park. Image by Benjamin Swift. “We used to harvest firewood from the Kewiña without replanting,” Andrea Vicente, a potato…
items.t: In the Bolivian Andes, Indigenous women plant native trees to restore water sources

items.title: Indigenous peoples leave collapsed climate talks with promises on hold
items.summary: ANTALYA, Türkiye — A year ago, a record number of Indigenous people attended the United Nations climate summit in Belém, Brazil. Although there as observers, without a seat at the negotiating table, they left with promises: recognition of their lands, a share of a new forest fund, and a just transition mechanism in the making. The 2026 climate conference, or COP31, that just concluded in Antalya, Türkiye — billed as the “implementation COP” — put those promises to the test. After two days of overtime, its main text collapsed. Narrower decisions survived, and some unresolved issues were pushed to next year’s climate meetings. Belém’s promises remain on hold. It was also meant to have a Pacific accent. Australia steered the negotiations, far from the other islands that had hoped to co-host. The region still made itself heard. In the closing plenary, the Marshall Islands and Vanuatu rejected the final text. Fiji and Tuvalu also voiced disappointment. For Indigenous delegates, Pacific Islanders among them, the question was whether Belém’s promises would turn into rights, funding, and a seat at the table. They came in numbers to find out. More than 350 were in the caucus in the first week, “a very big turnout,” Larissa Baldwin-Roberts, co-chair of the International Indigenous Peoples Forum on Climate Change (IIPFCC), told Mongabay. Delegates during the 2026 U.N. climate conference in Türkiye. Image by IISD/ENB – Mike Muzurakis. A push for rights recognition Among several demands, the IIPFCC caucus pressed one across the talks: to be…This article was originally published…
items.t: Indigenous peoples leave collapsed climate talks with promises on hold

items.title: Outcry grows over Labour plan to exempt most brownfield sites from nature protection rules
items.summary:
Chancellor’s decision to exempt plots up to 1.5 hectares allows developers to dodge rules aiming to reverse wildlife declines

An outcry is growing over the UK chancellor’s removal of most brownfield housing plots from a legal requirement for developers to measurably enhance nature.

John Healey’s decision in the budget to exempt brownfield plots of up to 1.5 hectares from biodiversity net gain (BNG) laws effectively means housing developers of inner-city, urban and surburban sites will be able to dodge rules designed to reverse steep wildlife declines while also allowing housebuilding growth. According to government data, 86% of brownfield sites currently registered are 1.5ha or under.

Continue reading...
items.t: Outcry grows over UK plan to exempt most brownfield sites from nature protection rules

items.title: Global marine conservation gathering seeks solutions amid mounting ocean challenges
items.summary: EDINBURGH — Ocean conservation efforts are being hindered by inadequate funding, as well as difficulties translating research into action, according to attendees of an international marine conservation congress in Scotland. Between Nov. 13 and 16, nearly 800 attendees from more than 65 countries convened in the Scottish capital, Edinburgh, for the eighth International Marine Conservation Congress (IMCC8). The conference is led by the Society for Conservation Biology (SCB), a U.S.-based international professional organization focused on the science and practice of conserving biodiversity. This year’s event brought together marine researchers, conservation practitioners, policymakers, journalists and others to discuss issues such as illegal fishing, sustainable fishing practices, marine protected areas (MPAs), community-led conservation efforts and deep-sea mining. Some presentations focused on solutions to reducing bycatch and illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing, while others discussed the successful implementations of MPAs. There were also sessions about ocean stewardship opportunities, how to use data to inform conservation and restoration efforts and ways to navigate science and policy in understanding deep-sea mining developments. Nearly 800 attendees from more than 65 countries convened in Edinburgh, Scotland, for IMCC8. Image courtesy of Cat Kutz/SCB Marine. Kathryn Matthews, chief scientist at the U.S.-headquartered ocean advocacy NGO Oceana, who was a plenary speaker at IMCC8, described the biennial event as a “congress unlike any other” due to the…
items.t: Global marine conservation gathering seeks solutions amid mounting ocean challenges

items.title: Indonesia fires test palm oil certification scheme as NGOs question RSPO accountability
items.summary: JAKARTA — Environmental groups are questioning the effectiveness of a global organization that develops standards and certification for sustainable palm oil production after fires affected thousands of hectares in concessions belonging to its members in Indonesia — including areas certified under its sustainability scheme. The criticism came as the organization, the Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil (RSPO), held its annual conference in Jakarta, which did not include a dedicated session on the country’s months-long fire and haze crisis. The fires have raised questions about whether the RSPO is doing enough to investigate affected concessions and to ensure that members meet their obligations to prevent and respond to fires, as well as protect forests, peatlands and wildlife habitat. Analysis conducted by Indonesian NGO Satya Bumi claims to have identified indications of fires, typically hotspots not yet subject to ground truthing, across 3,753 hectares (9,274 acres) of concessions belonging to 110 RSPO members in 19 Indonesian provinces. A separate analysis by NGO the Indonesian Forum for the Environment (Walhi) identifies 14 corporate groups and one company, including Singapore and Malaysia-registered companies, that are both RSPO members and linked to fire indicators: Genting Plantations, SD Guthrie, Kuala Lumpur Kepong, United Plantations, First Resources, Golden Agri-Resources, Musim Mas, Wilmar International, Astra Agro Lestari, Bumitama Agri, Prime Agri Resources, Sumber Tani Agung Resources, Sawit Sumbermas Sarana, Triputra Agro Persada and Palmina Utama.…
items.t: Indonesia fires test palm oil certification scheme as NGOs question RSPO accountability

items.title: Their loss changed Appalachian forests for ever. Now the American chestnut is back
items.summary:
The trees have been functionally extinct in the US for nearly a century. But new techniques are creating plants resistant to the parasitic blight that almost wiped them out

Jeff White is starstruck by a tree. The farmer and environmentalist from rural Maryland has an affinity with the American chestnut but has never seen one stretch from root to sky like this one. “About how tall is it?” he asks. “Over 70ft [21 metres],” says Cassie Stark, director of science implementation for the American Chestnut Foundation (TACF).

“Just incredible,” White says, his gaze fixed upwards. “I’ve never seen one so tall and so healthy.”

‘Thompson’, above left, is an unusually tall specimen of an American chestnut, a now-rare species once ubiquitous in the US. Jeff White next to ‘Gladys’, a thriving 15-metre-tall pure American Chestnut in Virginia’s Lesesne forest

items.t: Their loss changed Appalachian forests for ever. Now the American chestnut is back

items.title: Kiwi return to Wellington hills after 150 years in Māori-led conservation milestone
items.summary: For the first time in more than 150 years, wild kiwi are roaming the hills surrounding Aotearoa New Zealand’s capital city, Wellington. The milestone follows the reintroduction of more than 250 kiwi to the landscape, an effort led by Indigenous iwi (Māori nations), local community members and private landowners through the Capital Kiwi project, a nonprofit organization. Speaking on the Mongabay Newscast with host Mike DiGirolamo, project founder and lead Paul Ward explains that returning iconic flightless manu, or birds, to Wellington’s hills required extensive landscape-scale predator management. Stoats (Mustela erminea), small mammals that were introduced to Aotearoa New Zealand by Europeans in the late 1800s to control rabbit numbers, are the primary threats to young kiwi. So, before releasing the birds to the hills, project teams deployed more than 5,300 traps across 24,000 hectares (59,300 acres) of working farmland, and forestry and suburban reserves to trap and remove stoats. In areas without predator control, nearly all chicks die before reaching adulthood, Ward said, but under the project’s trapping regime, the chicks’ survival rate has exceeded 90%, he adds. Since late 2022, more than 250 kiwi have been translocated to the region. Including wild-hatched chicks, Ward estimates the local population now exceeds 300 birds. This “extraordinary result” is because the areas where the kiwi have been released have plenty of food for the birds, Ward says, “And so if you control or manage the predator threats, there are a heap of opportunities for our manu that are capable…
items.t: Kiwi return to Wellington hills after 150 years in Māori-led conservation milestone

items.title: 33 Of The Most Memorable Rescues By This Brazilian Lieutenant, From Orphaned Anteaters To Strays
items.summary:
As a 33-year-old officer with the Environmental Military Police in Minas Gerais, Brazil, Lieutenant Bernardo Bax spends his days shutting down illegal gold mines, enforcing fishing bans and going after people who keep wild birds in cages. But the side of his work that has won him more than 440,000 followers on Instagram, is much gentler: four baby toucans perched in his lap, a tiny owlet he named Fernanda, and a macaw that couldn’t stop playing with his mustache.

The clip that made many people fall for him shows a baby anteater orphaned after its mother was hit by a car. Instead of waiting in a transport box, the little one crawled inside Bax’s tactical vest, curled up against his chest and took a nap, as if it had decided a police officer would do just fine as a replacement parent. The cute moments are only half of what keeps viewers coming back. The lieutenant uses each rescue to teach something, from why the anteater wanted to cling to him to what you should do if you find a chick that has fallen from its nest.

Scroll down to see some of the sweetest rescues Bax and his team have shared, and tell us in the comments which of these little patients you’d happily let nap in your jacket.

items.title: Elders in Bali renew push against new offshore gas terminal
items.summary: DENPASAR, Indonesia — Customary leaders from Serangan village in Bali have renewed local opposition to a planned liquefied natural gas terminal off the east coast of the Indonesian island, saying the floating LNG site is too close to customary fishing grounds. “We disagree with the 3.5-kilometer distance [2.2 miles] because the vessel is large, and very close to the village’s sacred point as well as our fishing routes,” said I Nyoman Gede Pariartha, the traditional leader in Serangan, at a meeting on Nov. 14. Earlier this year Indonesia’s environment ministry issued an environmental permit for a Floating Storage and Regasification Unit (FSRU) off the eastern coast of Serangan island in Bali. The new infrastructure is intended to improve the reliability of Bali’s electricity supply by supplying gas-fired power plants amid rising electricity demand on the island. Bali has a population of 4.5 million, but the island received almost 7 million tourism visits in 2025 and, since the pandemic, has increasingly been host to longer-term visitors. Increasing electricity demand on the island is supplied by several power plants on Bali, including the gas-fired Pesanggaran power station, a 200 megawatt capacity facility next to a protected mangrove forest on the northern fringe of Benoa Bay. In addition, up to 30% of the island’s electricity is supplied by cables from neighboring Java, the world’s most populous island. The planned new FSRU site east of Bali will receive liquified natural gas offshore from tankers, and convert the fuel back into natural gas before supplying…This…
items.t: Elders in Bali renew push against new offshore gas terminal

items.title: Indonesian Borneo’s forests go quiet as smoke silences gibbons. Their singing matters
items.summary: Around dawn, a gibbon pair starts to sing. Their voices interweave, and the duet builds to a crescendo that fills the canopy. Across much of the Bornean forest, this is the sound of the morning. But since smoke from Indonesia’s worst fire crisis in over a decade has engulfed the island, forests have become noticeably quieter. On days when the haze is thick, the Borneo Nature Foundation (BNF) field team in Sebangau, Central Kalimantan, reports that gibbons sing less. Their songs sound shorter. Morning duets start later than usual, if they happen at all. Susan Cheyne, BNF’s co-director and vice-chair of the IUCN Primate Specialist Group Section on Small Apes, documented a similar pattern following forest fires in the same area in 2006. Researchers have yet to formally analyze their observations of the effects of this year’s fires, and will not be able to separate the different factors until the fires have subsided and fieldwork can resume. Cheyne believes several causes may be at play, with smoke — which irritates gibbons’ airways and reduces the light that cues morning duets — as a major driver. Bornean white-bearded gibbon (Hylobates albibarbis), Kalimantan Tengah, Indonesia. Image by © yannapis via iNaturalist (CC BY-NC 4.0). Why gibbon song matters Singing plays a central role in the social and reproductive lives of gibbons. Fiercely territorial, socially monogamous primates, they sing not only to attract mates, but also to defend their territory. Paired adults perform elaborate duets to demonstrate the strength of their bond and…This article was originally…
items.t: Indonesian Borneo’s forests go quiet as smoke silences gibbons. Their singing matter

items.title: Bush dogs are very rare. You’re 100x more likely to see a jaguar
items.summary: Founder’s Briefs: An occasional series where Mongabay founder Rhett Ayers Butler shares analysis, perspectives and story summaries. Biologists can spend decades working in the Amazon without seeing a bush dog. A new study quantifies just how rare the wild canids are. Writing in Canid Biology & Conservation, Robert Wallace and his colleagues at the Wildlife Conservation Society analyzed 25 years of camera-trap data from 97 sites across seven South American countries. In more than 2.1 million photographs, taken over 611,159 camera-trap nights, bush dogs (Speothos venaticus) appeared on just 12 occasions. Jaguars (Panthera onca) turned up about 100 times as often, and ocelots nearly 280 times. Even the short-eared dog (Atelocynus microtis), so fleetingly rare that it’s been nicknamed the “ghost dog,” was recorded 50 times as often as the bush dog. Bush dogs are found from Costa Rica to northeastern Argentina. They have short legs, weigh up to 7 kilograms (about 15 pounds), and sometimes hunt in packs of a dozen. In Brazil’s Cerrado, a single family group was found to occupy a home range of 140 square kilometers (54 square miles). In the latest study, the researchers analyzed footage from cameras mostly set 40–50 centimeters (16-20 inches) above the ground to photograph jaguars, which may have been a little high for bush dogs. Yet they readily photographed pacas, rodents of much the same size and shape as bush dogs, on nearly 40,000 occasions. A pack of dogs should also be easier to photograph than a solitary animal. The…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Bush dogs are very rare. You’re 100x more likely to see a jaguar

items.title: Timor-Leste issues guidelines for whale-watching, but malpractice is rife as industry booms
items.summary: DILI, Timor-Leste — As the annual whale migration gets into full swing in Timor-Leste, conservationists are raising concerns about increasingly aggressive tourist encounters with the world’s largest animals, despite new guidelines designed to protect them. Whale tourism is booming in a country whose waters are known as a “superhighway” for marine mammals. Migrating pygmy blue whales (Balaenoptera musculus brevicauda) are the star attraction for tourists seeking the experience of a lifetime. Though haze from wildfires in neighboring Indonesia made spotting whale spouts difficult in the earlier part of the season, industry-watchers have noticed a marked increase in the number of operators on the water this year. By the end of October, however, fewer whales had passed through the Ombai-Wetar Strait, which lies off the northern coast of Timor-Leste. This is likely because El Niño and the positive Indian Ocean Dipole have brought cooler waters in the region, delaying the migration of the whales, says cetacean ecologist Professor Karen Edyvane, who, in the past decade, has monitored migrating pygmy blue whales in Timor-Leste’s waters. This has meant more intense competition among whale tour operators to deliver experiences for customers, who pay $250-350 a day for the chance to swim with one of the few hundred pygmy blue whales that pass through each year. Industry-watchers have noticed cowboyish practices in the busiest season yet. Boats cutting across whales’ paths, operators pursuing mothers with calves, too many swimmers in the water at once — one tourist was taken out to…
items.t: Timor-Leste issues guidelines for whale-watching, but malpractice is rife as industry booms

items.title: Mongabay Kids launches Wild Guardians: A free education initiative to engage children with nature
items.summary: Mongabay Kids has launched Wild Guardians, a free multimedia educational series that connects upper elementary students with nature and inspires them to become stewards of wild things and wild places. Wild Guardians features stories of children and young people around the world working to protect their favorite animals and ecosystems. Through fun five-minute-long videos, illustrated comics and standards-aligned lessons and activities for fourth and fifth graders, Wild Guardians aims to bridge the gap between storytelling and environmental stewardship. The series features three different conservation topics: Restoring habitat for giraffes in Tanzania, the colorful world of wild bees and exploring and protecting waterways in Tennessee, U.S. Here are the adventures Wild Guardians takes children on: Growing food for giants Follow a group of primary school students in Tanzania who are growing food for giraffes and their community. Children will learn about how they can support their own local wildlife through tree planting, cleanups and habitat restoration. Exploring and protecting waterways Elementary students in Chattanooga, Tennessee, explore their local creek and watershed, home to wildlife such as the hellbender and crawfish. Children will learn that waterways connect landscapes, from mountains to sea, how human activities affect freshwater ecosystems and what they can do to help care for local waterways and the wildlife that depend on them. Discovering wild bees Students learn that there are more 20,000 species of bees, most of them wild bees that don’t produce honey.…
items.t: Mongabay Kids launches Wild Guardians: A free education initiative to engage children with nature

items.title: Longer droughts threaten floating health clinics as Amazon streams run dry
items.summary: RIO BRANCO, Brazil — The sun rises as the riverine healthcare crew starts disembarking medical supplies. They pass down boxes and coolers of all sizes from boat to canoe to smaller canoe, from the far end of the ship to the water’s edge, where a staff member with mud halfway up their shin will hand the load to the next on dry land to carry it uphill where the rest of the team is setting up today’s medical outpost. Every year, doctors, nurses, dentists and community health agents sail along Riozinho do Rôla, delivering medical care to the riverine population of the rural area of Rio Branco, capital of Acre state, in the Brazilian Amazon. Barro Alto, where the fleet is docked, is the first stop. Across the Amazon, a landscape of forests and rivers poses unique obstacles for accessing healthcare. “There are technical and operational challenges that are characteristic to this region,” nurse Alexandra Fernandes, who oversaw this year’s edition of Rio Branco’s healthcare flotilla, told Mongabay. In riverine communities like Barro Alto, isolated for months during wintertime floods, waterbound medical attention becomes a lifeboat. But with climate change and increasingly extreme drought seasons, channels that once connected people to the care they needed are now turning into barriers, as water gives way to mud. According to the November bulletin of the Drought and Immobility Risk in the Amazon Basin report, river levels across the Brazilian Amazon are “below or far below average.” In Acre alone, six of its 22…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Longer droughts threaten floating health clinics as Amazon streams run dry

items.title: China’s mangroves have bounced back. Birds have returned too
items.summary: Between 1998 and 2020, mangrove cover in China more than doubled, while the number of bird species recorded in those areas rose from 148 to 397, according to findings published in The Innovation. The recovery follows decades of steep decline: China lost nearly 70% of its mangroves between 1950 and 1990. Since then, the government has set aside mangrove reserves and restored degraded areas, including former aquaculture ponds. Rising temperatures and increased rainfall have also favored mangrove growth, according to the researchers. Image courtesy of Yang et al., 2026 (CC BY 4.0). The additional forest offers birds more nesting and roosting sites, and may have boosted populations of fish and other aquatic organisms on which many birds feed. The number of globally threatened bird species recorded in China’s mangrove habitats rose from 11 to 21 over the study period. Not all birds stand to benefit as the forests mature. Sandpipers and plovers feed on exposed mudflats and in openings among the trees. Both may become scarcer as mangroves grow denser. Elsewhere, too, mangroves are reclaiming lost ground. A study published in Science in June found that the world’s mangroves had been expanding since around 2010, offsetting much of the loss of the preceding decades. A separate assessment by Global Mangrove Watch found a net increase of 477 square kilometers (184 square miles) between 1985 and 2025 — a modest gain of 0.3% over four decades. Much of the new forest has grown without anyone planting a tree. Banner image: Mangroves…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: China’s mangroves have bounced back. Birds have returned too

items.title: A wake-up call for the UK government on wild birds | Letter
items.summary:
Emma Phipps of SongBird Survival writes that the government must act now to save woodland and farmland species from extinction

The Office for Environmental Protection’s finding that government departments are breaking the law by failing to protect wild birds should alarm us all (UK government ‘breaking the law’ by not stopping decline of wild birds, 18 November).

The scale of bird declines in the UK is impossible to ignore, and songbirds are among the worst affected. The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs’ wild bird indicators show that nearly 70% of farmland songbird species have declined since 1970. Woodland songbirds are faring little better, with more than 30% of species in decline. Unfortunately, none of this comes as a surprise. Decades of monitoring by scientists and dedicated volunteers have shown that our wild birds are in trouble. Yet successive governments have failed to act with the urgency needed to halt these declines.

items.title: In South Africa’s Limpopo, residents wonder what the next flood will bring
items.summary: “Everyone needs to understand their responsibilities before an emergency occurs.” This is the view of Hope Magidimisha, a national planning commissioner in the Office of the Presidency, South Africa. She said the January floods in South Africa’s Limpopo province, which is still feeling the effects, should serve as a reminder that disaster preparedness must begin long before heavy rains arrive. Some residents affected by the floods are still uncertain whether the repairs carried out since January will protect them when the next floods come. In Boelang, about 15 kilometers (9.3 miles) southwest of Ba-Phalaborwa, a municipality in Limpopo’s Mopani district, residents are once again fetching municipal water from their taps after infrastructure damaged by the January floods was repaired in March. Shanine (not her real name, due to safety concerns) told Mongabay that the repairs restored their water supply after the community had gone without municipal water for almost three months. However, she said water pressure remained unreliable, with water sometimes flowing slowly. “Our water infrastructure is right in the Selati River. The municipality has repaired it, but we are not sure how safe the structure is to withstand another flood,” she said. The January floods left a trail of destruction in Limpopo and disrupted learners from attending school and severely damaged water infrastructure in Boelang village. Two main pipelines crossing the Selati River at Boelang were washed away, while a pump station also failed. The damage left residents without municipal water for almost three…

items.title: Analysis: The collapse of UN climate talks, over fossil fuels, was years in the making
items.summary: NEW YORK (AP) — Going into this year’s U.N. climate talks in Turkey, expectations were notably low. Still, the outcome was even worse than expected—a failure to reach an overall agreement at a time of frequent extreme weather events fueled by climate change. While negotiations collapsed over one main point of contention—whether to include language about fossil fuels, the main driver of global warming—this fight over this has been building for many years. During previous conferences, nations frequently threatened to walk away if there wasn’t a strong agreement on fossil fuels. Instead, in the end, they voiced their disagreements in closing plenaries and ultimately got in line. This time, many countries were not willing to do that. Not just any quango, Natural England is the only public body that exists to legally protect the jewels in the crown of English nature – places increasingly under threat in a country that is overseeing an ongoing and devastating decline in its natural world.

Ecologists who work for Natural England are independent, and have the legal duty to scrutinise political decisions and ensure that short-term gallops for growth are not allowed to bulldoze forever rare and declining habitats.

items.title: Colombia president’s move on mining, oil weakens country’s Amazon protections, experts warn
items.summary: Colombia’s government, led by far-right President Abelardo De la Espriella, has sought to distance itself from the environmental policies of his 2022-2026 predecessor, left-wing Gustavo Petro, including those affecting the Amazon. The new administration in Bogotá recently repealed Resolution 0961, which prohibited large-scale mining and hydrocarbon extraction in this region, a move that experts say weakens protections not only for the biome but also for the Indigenous peoples who sustain it. The Ministry of Environment argues that the resolution was repealed because it was enacted without prior consultation with the region’s Afro-Colombian, Raizal and Palenquero traditional communities, and the measure does not, by itself, guarantee the Amazon biome’s protection. However, experts consulted by Mongabay say that, beyond repealing a measure — which was not the only one protecting the Amazon — the decision is also a political gesture that casts doubt on Colombia’s hard-won leadership in environmental protection. Organizations say that despite this leadership role, fossil fuel extraction and its infrastructure have accelerated forest loss in the Colombian Amazon, paving the way for other industries such as logging, mining and agriculture. A 2025 report by Earth Insight, the International Institute for Sustainable Development (IISD) and the National Organization of Indigenous Peoples of the Colombian Amazon (OPIAC) warns that 14 million hectares (34.6 million acres) of oil and gas blocks cover 28% of the Colombian Amazon — with 8 million hectares (19.8 million acres) overlapping…

items.title: Conservationists Bring Kiwi Back To New Zealand’s Capital, And The Birds Are Thriving
items.summary:
For around 150 years, the hills surrounding Wellington, New Zealand, were missing one very special sound: the call of a wild kiwi. These unusual birds, among the country’s most recognizable national symbols, disappeared from the area generations ago. But now, thanks to an ambitious conservation effort, they’re finally making a comeback.

Behind this success is the Capital Kiwi Project, founded by conservationist Paul Ward. Through years of predator control and cooperation with local communities, the project has helped bring kiwi back to the wild landscapes surrounding New Zealand’s capital, where the birds are once again living and breeding freely.

Scroll down to check out how the project moved along and read more about how it got to the point of reinstating a beloved native species.

More info: capitalkiwi.co.nz | Instagram | Facebook | youtube.com 

Before kiwi could return to Wellington’s hills, the Capital Kiwi Project had to tackle one of the biggest threats to their survival: introduced predators 

Capital Kiwi Project 

Trap deployment, Pipinui Point, 2019

Photo by Josiah Watson

Kiwi are unlike most other birds. They’re flightless, mostly nocturnal, and covered in hair-like feathers. They also have long, sensitive beaks with nostrils near the tips, allowing them to sniff out insects, worms, and other food beneath the ground. Found naturally only in New Zealand, these curious-looking birds are also deeply connected to the country’s cultural identity.

Beginning in 2019, the team established a predator-control network that would…

The archipelago, a British overseas territory claimed by Argentina, is home to large colonies of albatrosses and penguins. Its waters, with those of the Patagonian shelf, provide feeding grounds for sea lions, southern elephant seals and southern right whales.

items.title: Country diary 1906: Peace reigns again in the deer park
items.summary:
28 November 1906: A month ago the hart roared a deep challenge; now he does not threaten but trots with dignity towards his harem

What a difference a few weeks make to the behaviour of the park stags. A month ago, if approached, the excited hart angrily scraped the ground, swelled his shaggy neck, and, lowering his head, coughed defiance or roared that deep, far-sounding challenge. One felt it wise to give him antler-room and leave him to guard his more nervous hinds. Now, though the great beasts are not so timid as the fallow bucks, he does not threaten, but, standing at gaze, waits until we come near; then, wheeling, he trots with dignity towards his harem, turning occasionally to see if we are following. When we have passed he calmly turns his attention once more to the rough park grass. The hinds are won and the annual battles are over; even the silly fellows have ceased to grunt and run aimlessly amongst the trees; peace reigns in the park until next autumn.

An interesting hedgehog story has been sent to me. At a country house near Malvern the cats are fed out of doors from a large dish. Regularly a wild hedgehog comes to the dish and feeds, unmolested by the cats; probably the well-fed cats look upon the hedgehog as an inhabitant of the garden and not as game. This is curious, but not so strange when we consider what a well-armed animal the hedgehog is. Last week, however, the hedgehog brought with it to the dish a young one, but the cats, probably because they were used to the presence of the mother, did not attack the toothsome…

items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising reason why early life may have survived Earth's intense ultraviolet radiation: a key component of DNA appears to turn potentially destructive damage into something easier to repair. items.title: A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA
items.summary: At an astonishing 194 years old, Jonathan the giant tortoise is the world's oldest living land animal, and scientists may have finally uncovered the secrets behind his extraordinary lifespan. Researchers identified 287 unique genetic variants linked to processes that help repair damaged DNA, control inflammation, regulate insulin, and suppress cancer.

items.title: A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along
items.summary: A decades-old theory suggesting that evolution protects its most important genes from mutations has been dealt a major blow. An extensive new analysis of mutations in bacteria and yeast found no evidence that essential genes mutate less frequently than other genes. Researchers say earlier studies may have been misled by harmful mutations that disappeared through natural selection before scientists could detect them.

items.title: Scientists say the human family tree may need a radical rewrite
items.summary: The human family tree may need a major overhaul. New research from Monash University challenges the traditional classification of our ancient ancestors, arguing that species such as Australopithecus and Paranthropus should be grouped within our own genus, Homo. As scientists uncover more fossils and analyze evolutionary relationships, the boundaries that once separated these ancient relatives are becoming increasingly difficult to defend.

items.title: ‘People couldn’t deal with watching an animal die’: the strange saga of Timmy the whale – and how a whole country lost its mind
items.summary:
When the humpback got stranded on Germany’s Baltic coast, crowds gathered, conspiracy theorists pitted themselves against scientists and animal lovers argued with vets. Why did the animal trigger such an intense derangement?

What surprised Bodo Köpnick was how loud the whale was. “You could hear it as far away as the next village. It was eerie, but also impressive,” he says, then pauses to think how best to describe the noise a suffering humpback makes at night. “It was like a cow moaning. It went to your marrow.”

Köpnick, 65, is everything you would hope for in a volunteer fire chief on a sleepy holiday island: a grandfatherly figure who mostly spends his weekends teaching local children about health and safety, and letting them climb on the engines. But on 31 March his life was made infinitely more stressful by the appearance of a lost whale that had got itself stranded on the shores of his island of Poel, in northern Germany. It became his fate to stand on the shoreline and guard the huge creature while behind him an entire country lost its mind.

items.title: Country diary: Watching a garden spider at work – do I detect a personality? | Oliver Southall
items.summary:
Hurstpierpoint, West Sussex: The way that it sits patiently, and solves problems … it’s hard not to wonder if it has some kind of inner life

Three months with a newborn has given me a fresh perspective on nature. What will Tom enjoy out here, I wonder, as we step outside. I hold him under trees and watch his astonished eyes. Every morning, as a hopeful inoculation against arachnophobia, I show him the garden spider (Araneus diadematus) outside our back window. Is that a smile?

Attending to a baby’s developing preferences has got me thinking about what makes an individual creature unique. Recently I learned that Len Howard – whose 1952 book Birds As Individuals lovingly described the quirks of her garden tits and thrushes – lived nearby. Contemporary experiments with honeybees have shown that diversity in workers’ personality traits makes for an adaptable and resilient hive.

items.title: Autopsy Results Reveal What Really Happened To Fiona The Hippo, As Witnesses Speak Out On Freak Accident
items.summary:
The autopsy results for Fiona the hippo have finally been released, giving more details about what happened inside her body after she swallowed a visitor’s knitted hat. 

The nine-year-old Cincinnati Zoo favorite passed away on November 19, despite her caretakers trying several ways to save her. 

Now, the zoo has shared the findings of her examination, explaining why the veterinary team couldn’t remove the object and why even continued treatment wouldn’t have changed the outcome. 

Autopsy results revealed how the hat became stuck inside Fiona and couldn’t be removed 

On Friday, November 20, Cincinnati Zoo released the results of Fiona’s necropsy, the term for an animal autopsy. 

The examination revealed that the knitted hat had become lodged in the middle of her small intestine . It was approximately 25 feet beyond her final stomach compartment and 50 feet from the end of her intestines. 

This meant the object was stuck in a part of her digestive system the veterinary team could not reach with the equipment available.

items.summary:
Scientists reared the San Francisco natives through their vulnerable youth before setting them free in nature

San Francisco garter snakes born and raised in a zoo-based conservation program have been released into the wild for the first time as part of an effort to save what is considered one of North America’s most beautiful snakes.

The non-venomous reptiles are known for their striking colors – red heads, turquoise bellies and vibrant red and black stripes on their sides. The species, found only on the San Francisco peninsula, has been listed as endangered for more than half a century.

items.title: How the war in Iran turned the Gulf into a climate catastrophe – video explainer
items.summary:
The war between the US, Israel and Iran has turned the strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s busiest oil shipping routes, into a battlefield, but also the centre of a deepening environmental disaster. Tankers struck by missiles or sea mines are leaking oil into the Gulf, leaving vast slicks visible from space, staining coastlines and threatening lasting damage to marine ecosystems. Many of these areas remain inaccessible because of the naval blockade, making it virtually impossible to document the devastation on the ground.
